hypothesis: The aqueous-phase metabolite feature with molecular formula C14H20N4O3S is increased/characteristic in 12-month-old infants fed dairy-based complementary protein relative to meat-based complementary protein.
rationale: This feature is annotation-free: it is defined only by a molecular formula (C14H20N4O3S), with no compound name, HMDB/KEGG/ChEBI identifier, adduct, or retention-time information. Searches on the formula itself returned only synthetic/pharmaceutical matches (e.g. vendor listings of an N-nitroso sumatriptan impurity of the same formula, MW 324.4, and an unnamed PubChem CID 6786786 entry) and Wikipedia formula-index pages for neighbouring formulas - i.e. no endogenous, dietary, or microbially derived metabolite could be confidently assigned, and no HMDB/food-metabolite record surfaced. Formula-space checks against plausible sulfur/nitrogen-rich endogenous candidates did not fit: Met-His and His-Met dipeptides are C11H18N4O3S (ChEBI:74703 / CHEBI:74053) and Ala-His-Met is C14H23N5O4S, so the obvious sulfur-amino-acid peptide interpretations are excluded by hydrogen/nitrogen count. Consequently there is no identified compound about which to search feature-specific literature, and no pathway to reason from. Literature on the exposure itself does exist (the Denver/Colorado randomized meat- vs dairy-based complementary feeding trial in formula-fed infants from 5 to 12 months, with fecal microbiome, SCFA, serum metabolomics, and a network-representation-learning multi-omics analysis: e.g. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9909089/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7912106/, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.11.01.621627v3), but none of these reports any metabolite matching C14H20N4O3S as dairy-associated; the dairy-classified metabolites highlighted in the multi-omics preprint were lipids (a C20 sphingoid base and a hydroxy-sulfatide), not a sulfur/nitrogen heterocyclic aqueous compound. Because zero literature was located for this specific feature (identified or formula-matched) in any infant, dairy, or gut context, the correct score under the rubric is 0 (none found) rather than 1, since not even generic pathway-level reasoning is possible for an unassigned formula.
contradicting_evidence: No literature reporting this feature in the opposite direction was found either, so the score is 'none found' rather than 'contradicting'. Worth noting as context, not contradiction: the serum untargeted/targeted metabolomics analysis of the meat- vs dairy-based complementary feeding trial (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7912106/) reported that no metabolites differentiated the meat and dairy groups after correction for multiple testing at 12 months, a point reiterated in the companion gut microbiota paper (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9909089/). That is a serum, annotated-metabolite null result and does not directly speak to an unannotated fecal/aqueous feature, but it lowers the prior that any single protein-source-discriminating small molecule at 12 months is well established in the published record.

caveats: The main limitation is chemical ambiguity: a molecular formula alone can correspond to many isomers (peptide-like, purine/pteridine-like, thiazole/thiamine-like, or exogenous/xenobiotic species), and one of the few concrete hits for C14H20N4O3S was a drug-related impurity, which raises the possibility that this feature is a xenobiotic, adduct/in-source fragment, or artefact rather than an endogenous or diet-derived metabolite. Literature confidence cannot be raised above 0 until the feature is annotated (MS2 spectrum, accurate-mass/adduct assignment, authentic standard, or database match). Recommended next steps: confirm the adduct and neutral mass, search MS2 against GNPS/mzCloud/HMDB, and only then re-run a feature-specific literature search using the resolved compound name; also check whether the feature co-elutes with known dairy-related sulfur/nitrogen compounds (e.g. thiamine derivatives, methionine-containing peptides from casein/whey hydrolysis) since those would give a testable mechanistic hypothesis for a dairy-protein effect.
